title: Global Strategy Competing Around the World

questions.stem: A belief that EV buyers’ preferences are converging worldwide best supports which idea?

options.A: Globalization hypothesis: preferences converge, enabling standardized offerings worldwide over time
options.B: Porter diamond: factor conditions alone explain global demand for vehicles
options.C: Death-of-distance hypothesis: geography stops affecting competitive advantage today at all
options.D: Liability-of-foreignness thesis: entrants enjoy lower costs in new markets always

questions.explanation: The globalization hypothesis posits converging consumer preferences across countries, encouraging standardized offerings. The death-of-distance hypothesis is about geography no longer driving advantage; the other options are mismatched.

questions.stem: A full manufacturing-and-sales ‘replica’ of the firm in a few key foreign countries is most consistent with which stage of globalization?

options.A: Globalization 3.0: globally distributed network of excellence everywhere
options.B: Globalization 3.1: retrenchment with rapid reshoring domestically alone
options.C: Globalization 2.0: mini-replicas with most functions abroad operating
options.D: Globalization 1.0: exports with limited overseas functions only

questions.explanation: Globalization 2.0 is characterized by creating smaller, self-contained copies of the firm abroad to increase local responsiveness, funded by significant FDI. Globalization 1.0 is export-led; 3.0 is networked and polycentric.

questions.stem: A partial rollback of global integration driven by nationalism and trade frictions is labelled in the chapter as:

options.A: Globalization 3.1, a period of retrenchment now
options.B: Globalization 4.0, a period of full autarky
options.C: Globalization 2.1, a period of hyper-integration now
options.D: Globalization 1.1, a period of decolonisation now

questions.explanation: The chapter discusses a post-3.0 period of retrenchment—sometimes framed as Globalization 3.1—marked by rising protectionism, trade wars, and geopolitical fragmentation.

questions.stem: Among the classic ‘why go global’ motives, BYD’s Hungary move most directly serves which one?

options.A: Access a larger market by lowering barriers to entry there
options.B: Access low-cost inputs by moving production to cheaper labor there
options.C: Develop new competencies by joining advanced EV engineering clusters there
options.D: Boost reputation by signalling compliance with European regulators and jobs

questions.explanation: A European plant can be a strategic commitment that deepens market access by reducing policy and logistics barriers. While cost and reputation effects may follow, the clearest motive is strengthening the competitive position in a large market.

questions.stem: BYD uses a common vehicle platform but tailors financing, software, and bundles by country. Which global strategy is closest?

options.A: Global standardization: single model set, strong global integration
options.B: International strategy: export platform, minimal local adaptation only
options.C: Multidomestic strategy: national units tailor vehicles and marketing
options.D: Transnational strategy: integrated platform plus deep country tailoring

questions.explanation: A transnational strategy aims to achieve both high cost efficiency (shared platforms, scale, integrated operations) and high local responsiveness (country-specific compliance, go-to-market, complements).

questions.stem: BYD’s announced Szeged (Hungary) facility is best classified as which foreign-entry mode?

options.A: Equity joint venture with a Hungarian state partner
options.B: Non-equity licensing to a Hungarian contract assembler firm
options.C: Wholly owned greenfield subsidiary for EU vehicle assembly
options.D: Wholly owned acquisition of an EU vehicle assembler

questions.explanation: A new factory built and owned by the entrant is a greenfield subsidiary. It requires high capital, but gives BYD maximal operational control over quality, compliance, and proprietary manufacturing know-how compared with exporting, licensing, or a joint venture.

questions.stem: BYD’s decision to manufacture in the EU is primarily a response to:

options.A: Higher cost-reduction pressure created by tariffs and logistics costs
options.B: Lower local-responsiveness pressure due to EU harmonization trends now
options.C: Higher local-responsiveness pressure from diverse European driving norms today
options.D: Lower cost-reduction pressure due to protected domestic competitors only

questions.explanation: Local production can directly reduce tariff and logistics costs, increasing cost efficiency. It may also support responsiveness, but the primary trigger in the caselet is the tariff-driven cost shock.

questions.stem: BYD’s investment in a Hungarian manufacturing facility is best described as:

options.A: Portfolio investment in foreign equities without operational control
options.B: International licensing allowing others to manufacture under brand
options.C: Foreign direct investment in overseas value chain activities
options.D: Cross-border exporting using home-country production and shipping only

questions.explanation: FDI is investment in value-chain activities abroad (e.g., plants, R&D, distribution). Exporting sells across borders without investment in foreign operations; portfolio investment lacks operational control; licensing transfers rights to a partner.

questions.stem: Even with local EU assembly, which CAGE dimension is typically least ‘solved’ for a new foreign auto brand?

options.A: Geographic distance in delivery times between EU capitals still
options.B: Cultural distance in trust, brand meaning, and car habits
options.C: Economic distance in income, financing, and wage levels locally
options.D: Administrative distance from EU tariffs on China imports anyway

questions.explanation: Local assembly can reduce geographic frictions and sometimes administrative ones (e.g., import duties), but it does not automatically erase cultural distance—brand legitimacy, preferences, and norms that shape adoption and dealer/service expectations.

questions.stem: Evidence that only 10–25% of activity is cross-border most directly challenges the claim that:

options.A: That domestic demand has no influence on national competitive advantage today
options.B: That cross-border trade makes firms unable to protect their IP ever
options.C: That borders barely matter because the world is fully flat now
options.D: That every major company earns most revenue outside home markets already

questions.explanation: Low cross-border shares imply the world is only semi-globalized, contradicting the ‘fully flat’ narrative. The other statements are not the primary implication of the semi-globalization evidence.

questions.stem: Hungary’s skilled workforce, infrastructure, and incentives map most directly onto which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Related industries: strong complementors like batteries and charging networks
options.B: Demand conditions: sophisticated home customers pushing EV innovation fast
options.C: Factor conditions: skilled labor, infrastructure, and supportive institutions there
options.D: Competitive intensity: fierce local rivals forcing continuous improvement there

questions.explanation: Factor conditions cover a nation’s endowments—human capital, infrastructure, capital markets, and institutional support. Demand conditions and rivalry intensity describe different diamond elements.

questions.stem: If BYD must keep costs low while tailoring compliance and offers by country, which global strategy best fits?

options.A: Global standardization: one EU model, centralized operations, maximal scale effects
options.B: International strategy: export vehicles, relying on home-based strengths to Europe
options.C: Transnational strategy: shared platform plus tailored compliance and offers across
options.D: Multidomestic strategy: independent country units redesign vehicles locally each year

questions.explanation: High pressure for cost reductions plus high pressure for local responsiveness points to a transnational strategy, which seeks global integration and local adaptation simultaneously—hard to execute but potentially powerful.

questions.stem: If BYD wanted immediate local distribution assets and market knowledge, which high-control entry mode is most aligned?

options.A: Build a greenfield plant to develop capabilities slowly there
options.B: Acquire an existing automaker to obtain assets quickly there
options.C: Export finished cars to test demand before investing there
options.D: Form licensing deal transferring IP with low control there

questions.explanation: Acquisition can deliver speed—existing assets, permits, workforce, and channels—at the cost of integration risk and acquisition premiums. Greenfield offers control but slower ramp; exporting and licensing provide lower control.

questions.stem: If BYD’s priority is IP protection and end-to-end quality control, which entry approach fits best?

options.A: Build a wholly owned greenfield plant with integrated sales in Europe
options.B: Create a fifty-fifty joint venture with an established OEM in Europe
options.C: License designs to a local contract manufacturer for assembly in Europe
options.D: Export from China, relying on independent distributors for servicing in Europe

questions.explanation: Moving to a wholly owned subsidiary (especially greenfield) increases control, which protects IP and brand standards. Exporting and licensing cede more control to partners; a 50–50 JV creates shared control and greater leakage/coordination risks.

questions.stem: Import duties that compress margins primarily increase which pressure in the cost–responsiveness framework?

options.A: Lowers cost-reduction pressure by protecting high-cost incumbents in Europe now
options.B: Raises local-responsiveness pressure by shifting consumer tastes rapidly there today
options.C: Raises cost-reduction pressure by shrinking margins on imported vehicles directly
options.D: Lowers local-responsiveness pressure by unifying EU regulations further over time

questions.explanation: Tariffs raise the effective cost of serving the market via imports, which heightens pressure for cost reductions (or for alternative structures such as local production) to protect margins.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s description of a ‘techno cold war’, which technology bundle is explicitly central?

options.A: 5G networks, AI robotics, and quantum computing leadership race
options.B: Oil pipelines, crop yields, and steel furnaces leadership race
options.C: Tourism visas, art exports, and language schools leadership race
options.D: Airlines routes, port fees, and hotel chains leadership race

questions.explanation: The techno cold war is framed as competition for leadership in strategically important technologies—examples include 5G, AI/robotics, and quantum computing—because these shape economic and security power.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s ‘semi-globalized’ snapshot, what share of investment is foreign direct investment (FDI)?

options.A: Eighteen percent of investments are foreign direct investments
options.B: Six percent of investments are foreign direct investments
options.C: Nine percent of investments are foreign direct investments
options.D: Fifteen percent of investments are foreign direct investments

questions.explanation: The chapter argues the world is only semi-globalized and uses a set of low cross-border shares; one of them is that only about 9% of investments are FDI.

questions.stem: Moving from exporting toward acquisitions/greenfields along the entry-mode continuum typically implies:

options.A: Higher control, less IP leakage, but more capital committed upfront overall risk
options.B: Lower control, faster exit, but more tariff exposure and disputes with partners
options.C: Higher control, faster learning, but lower fixed costs per unit from scale
options.D: Lower control, wider reach, but stronger global brand protection at entry time

questions.explanation: Higher-investment modes raise control (helping brand and IP protection) but require major capital commitments and carry integration/coordination risk. Lower-investment modes are more reversible but expose the firm to partner and policy risks.

questions.stem: The EU’s anti-subsidy duties most directly increase which CAGE ‘distance’ for a China-based EV exporter?

options.A: Administrative distance via regulation, tariffs, and enforcement uncertainty today
options.B: Economic distance in income levels, credit access, and wages
options.C: Cultural distance in language, values, and consumption norms abroad
options.D: Geographic distance in shipping time, ports, and logistics routes

questions.explanation: Tariffs and trade remedies are political-administrative barriers, raising administrative distance (rules, enforcement risk, policy volatility). They do not primarily change miles travelled (geographic), income levels (economic), or cultural norms.

questions.stem: The added costs of operating in unfamiliar local institutions are best captured by which concept?

options.A: Liability of foreignness from operating in unfamiliar institutions abroad
options.B: Economies of scale from spreading fixed costs globally widely
options.C: Experience curve from cumulative output lowering unit cost steadily
options.D: Location economies from placing factories near optimal input factors

questions.explanation: Liability of foreignness refers to the extra costs of doing business in unfamiliar cultural/economic environments and coordinating across distance. The other options describe cost advantages, not penalties.

questions.stem: The chapter’s ‘systemic rivalry’ framing (EU–China shift) is best described as:

options.A: Systemic rivalry pits democratic markets against state-managed capitalism in trade and technology policy
options.B: Systemic rivalry refers to geographic distance increasing as transport costs rise again today
options.C: Systemic rivalry describes cultural clashes that vanish when tariffs are removed quickly everywhere
options.D: Systemic rivalry means firms compete only on price within a single market today

questions.explanation: Systemic rivalry refers to competition between political-economic systems and governance models, not just firm-level price rivalry or geography. It can drive policy barriers, investment screening, and strategic decoupling pressures.

questions.stem: What is the most typical trade-off when switching from exporting to EU-based greenfield manufacturing?

options.A: Lower tariff exposure, higher fixed costs, and harder cross-border coordination across functions overall
options.B: Higher tariff exposure, lower fixed costs, and simpler coordination through one hub overall
options.C: Higher tariff exposure, higher fixed costs, and harder coordination due to licensing abroad
options.D: Lower tariff exposure, lower fixed costs, and simpler coordination through outsourcing partners abroad

questions.explanation: Local manufacturing can reduce tariff and shipping exposure, but it introduces fixed-cost commitments and coordination complexity across the multinational network (suppliers, HQ, multiple markets).

questions.stem: Which action most clearly reduces costs (C) rather than increasing value (V) under tariffs?

options.A: Sponsor charging stations to increase adoption and perceived ecosystem in Europe widely
options.B: Shift assembly inside EU to lower tariff-related costs per unit sold there
options.C: Spend on branding to improve legitimacy with skeptical regulators in Europe first
options.D: Add premium features to justify higher prices despite tariffs in Europe now

questions.explanation: Relocating assembly to avoid tariffs and reduce logistics costs is a direct cost reduction lever. The other actions primarily seek to raise customer willingness to pay or legitimacy (value creation), not reduce unit costs.

questions.stem: Which entry-mode rule-of-thumb is correctly stated in the chapter’s menu of options?

options.A: Joint ventures suit products; exporting suits services using outlets abroad
options.B: Licensing suits services; franchising suits products using patents abroad today
options.C: Acquisitions suit services; alliances suit products using tariffs abroad now
options.D: Licensing suits products; franchising suits services using brand standards abroad

questions.explanation: Licensing typically applies to product-related IP (e.g., patents/technology), while franchising is often used for services where the brand and operating system are replicated through franchisees.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly distinguishes CAGE from liability of foreignness?

options.A: CAGE captures operating costs; liability guides the country selection decision for entrants
options.B: CAGE reduces tariffs; liability explains why trade barriers disappear worldwide over time
options.C: CAGE predicts profits; liability measures rivalry intensity among global firms in markets
options.D: CAGE guides country choice; liability captures added operating costs abroad for entrants

questions.explanation: CAGE is a decision framework for ‘where’ to compete by assessing relative distance. Liability of foreignness is a cost disadvantage experienced once operating abroad, due to unfamiliarity and coordination across distance.

questions.stem: A SaaS startup sells subscriptions to U.S. customers from India with no local presence. Which foreign-entry mode is closest?

options.A: Joint venture with local firm sharing governance equally
options.B: Franchising outlets to local operators in target markets
options.C: Exporting services digitally from home base to customers
options.D: Greenfield subsidiary building local facilities from scratch there

questions.explanation: Exporting can apply to digital services as cross-border delivery from the home base. The other options imply partner governance or owned local facilities.

questions.stem: A large, demanding domestic smartphone market that pressures firms on features and value maps to which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Related industries from complementors like logistics and payments ecosystems
options.B: Demand conditions from large, price-sensitive, feature-comparing home buyers there
options.C: Competitive intensity from strong local rivals pushing efficiency continuously
options.D: Factor conditions from rare minerals uniquely available domestically there

questions.explanation: Demand conditions emphasize the sophistication and characteristics of home-market demand that push firms toward innovation and efficiency. Factor conditions and related industries are separate diamond elements.

questions.stem: A multi-country, ‘follow-the-activity’ supply chain spanning China, India, and end-markets is most characteristic of:

options.A: Globalization 2.0 with self-contained replicas in few countries today
options.B: Globalization 3.1 with complete reshoring and closed borders today
options.C: Globalization 1.0 with exports and home-based production only today
options.D: Globalization 3.0 with globally distributed value-chain collaboration networks today

questions.explanation: Globalization 3.0 emphasizes global collaboration networks that locate functions worldwide for an optimal cost–capability–PESTEL mix, rather than simple exports or self-contained replicas.

questions.stem: A premium product sold worldwide with limited local adaptation and low cost pressure most closely reflects which global strategy?

options.A: Global standardization: compete on lowest cost via centralized production
options.B: Transnational strategy: optimize costs while tailoring deeply to locals
options.C: Multidomestic strategy: redesign product uniquely for each country market
options.D: International strategy: leverage home-based competencies with limited adaptation globally

questions.explanation: An international strategy leverages home-based core competencies into foreign markets, often with relatively limited adaptation. It fits when pressures for both local responsiveness and cost reductions are comparatively low.

questions.stem: A shift from multilateral trade deals toward bilateral rules tends to raise what for MNEs?

options.A: Lower geographic distance because new ports reduce travel miles worldwide today
options.B: Greater policy uncertainty as trade rules vary across bilateral agreements now
options.C: Lower administrative distance because one global treaty sets uniform rules everywhere
options.D: Greater cultural convergence as firms standardize products across nations quickly now

questions.explanation: Bilateralism can fragment trade rules, increasing administrative complexity and uncertainty for MNEs that operate across many jurisdictions, compared with stable multilateral frameworks.

questions.stem: A ‘global collaboration network’ logic implies a firm locates each function based on:

options.A: Locate R&D abroad but keep marketing identical for all customers
options.B: Locate all functions domestically to maximize one-way knowledge flow only
options.C: Locate functions globally using optimal cost–capability–PESTEL mix for each activity
options.D: Locate only sales abroad while keeping production strictly at home

questions.explanation: Global collaboration networks place activities wherever they best fit the cost, capability, and broader contextual (PESTEL) profile—rather than defaulting to a single-country configuration.

questions.stem: Adding local payment integrations and India-specific compliance features mainly uses local responsiveness to reinforce:

options.A: Local responsiveness supports differentiation by tailoring features to local needs more
options.B: Local responsiveness supports cost leadership by standardizing features globally even more
options.C: Cost reductions support focus strategy by narrowing markets to one segment
options.D: Cost reductions support differentiation by increasing product variety across countries always

questions.explanation: Local responsiveness typically increases differentiation by tailoring the offering to local preferences and requirements. Cost reductions, by contrast, often support cost leadership through standardization and scale.

questions.stem: An MNE that draws innovation from several equally important hubs (rather than a single HQ) is pursuing:

options.A: One-way innovation strategy exporting HQ ideas to subsidiaries only
options.B: Polycentric innovation strategy using multiple equally important global hubs
options.C: Globalization 1.0 production strategy with domestic-only R&D functions only
options.D: Multidomestic sales strategy with independent marketing in each country

questions.explanation: Polycentric innovation involves multiple innovation hubs contributing meaningfully to the firm’s innovation flow, replacing a one-way HQ-to-subsidiary model.

questions.stem: Apple’s India assembly move is least directly aimed at which advantage of competing internationally in the chapter’s list?

options.A: Accessing a larger end-market because India replaces U.S. demand growth for iPhones
options.B: Developing new competencies by embedding suppliers into a new ecosystem for assembly
options.C: Hedging policy shocks by reducing dependence on one jurisdiction for production risk
options.D: Accessing low-cost inputs and incentives to improve unit economics for iPhones abroad

questions.explanation: The chapter lists three main advantages: larger markets, low-cost inputs, and new competencies. The India shift is primarily about production risk/cost and policy hedging; it is not mainly about replacing U.S. demand with Indian demand.

questions.stem: Assume Apple expands India output mainly through contract manufacturers who own the plants. For Apple, this is best described as:

options.A: Apple’s FDI in India: it owns plants and operations directly there
options.B: Pure exporting: Apple makes iPhones domestically and ships abroad to India
options.C: Portfolio approach: Apple buys minority stakes without operational control in India
options.D: Outsourced global production; not Apple-owned FDI, but partner expansion in India

questions.explanation: FDI requires the focal firm to invest in and control value-chain activity abroad. If partners own the factories and Apple simply contracts with them, Apple is using global outsourcing within a global strategy, while the partners may be the ones making FDI.

questions.stem: If Apple wants strict control over retail experience in India (pricing, service rituals, brand standards), which entry approach best fits?

options.A: Franchising to independent operators to localize experience and staffing fully
options.B: Wholly owned retail subsidiary to standardize customer experience and pricing
options.C: Licensing retail IP to local firms without ongoing oversight today
options.D: Exporting devices only, avoiding any owned presence in-market at all

questions.explanation: Higher control entry modes (owned subsidiaries) reduce brand and service variance. Franchising and licensing allow faster expansion but cede more control and raise reputational risk.

questions.stem: If a host country requires a joint venture for smartphone manufacturing, which risk rises most sharply according to the chapter’s warning?

options.A: Lower market risk because tariffs disappear once joint venture signed
options.B: Higher IP exposure as partners can learn and reverse-engineer designs
options.C: Higher market size because joint ventures automatically expand demand rapidly
options.D: Lower IP exposure because partnership prevents any knowledge transfer outward

questions.explanation: Forced partnering can expose proprietary know-how to leakage and reverse engineering. This is a classic disadvantage of global expansion when host-country rules mandate local partners.

questions.stem: If bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent enforcement slow equipment movement into India, which CAGE dimension is most directly increasing?

options.A: Cultural distance rises when both countries share the same language
options.B: Geographic distance rises when aircraft fly faster between two cities
options.C: Administrative distance rises when regulations, approvals, and enforcement become uncertain
options.D: Economic distance rises when wage levels converge across two markets

questions.explanation: Administrative and political distance captures differences in rules, institutions, and enforcement. Bureaucratic uncertainty and inconsistent approvals raise this distance and thus the costs and risks of operating.

questions.stem: If poor working conditions at an India-based supplier trigger global backlash, which ‘disadvantage of going global’ is most implicated?

options.A: Loss of reputation from stakeholder backlash about labor practices
options.B: Liability of foreignness from unfamiliar retail norms overseas alone
options.C: Loss of IP from reverse engineering of chip designs
options.D: Location economies from clustering production near leading R&D hubs

questions.explanation: Reputational loss can follow from sourcing or labor controversies in global supply chains. This is distinct from IP leakage risks or generic coordination costs.

questions.stem: India-based assembly is sensible on cost grounds when:

options.A: When India’s assembly costs exceed tariff savings but reputation improves slightly overall
options.B: When geographic distance shrinks because India is closer to China by sea
options.C: When cultural distance dominates and tariffs are irrelevant for profits now overall
options.D: When tariff savings exceed India’s extra assembly costs and coordination burdens overall

questions.explanation: The shift is economically justified if it lowers the all-in cost of serving the target market after accounting for tariffs, logistics, learning-curve effects, and coordination costs.

questions.stem: Locating final assembly in India to improve the risk-adjusted cost position is best captured by which concept?

options.A: Globalization hypothesis by standardizing tastes in all countries quickly
options.B: Location economies by placing assembly where total costs fall
options.C: Demand conditions by serving sophisticated domestic Indian customers first
options.D: Learning effects by producing more units at one site

questions.explanation: Location economies are benefits from placing a value-chain activity in the geography that offers the best mix of costs, capabilities, and contextual factors (including policy risk).

questions.stem: Relative to China-based assembly under tariff and export-control pressure, Apple’s India pivot is most directly a response to which CAGE dimension?

options.A: Economic distance: wage levels converging between India and China rapidly
options.B: Administrative distance: tariff regimes and export restrictions driving redesign choices
options.C: Geographic distance: sea routes shortening dramatically via Indian ports today
options.D: Cultural distance: American consumers rejecting products assembled in China openly

questions.explanation: The trigger in the caselet is policy risk: tariffs, export rules, and government frictions. Those are administrative/political distance issues, even if the move also affects cost and logistics.

questions.stem: The chapter notes that high-control foreign acquisitions can reduce exposure to which two downsides of global business?

options.A: High-control acquisitions can reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners
options.B: Franchising contracts always reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners
options.C: Licensing contracts always reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners
options.D: Low-control exporting can reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners

questions.explanation: Higher control reduces reliance on external partners for quality and proprietary know-how. Exporting, licensing, and franchising typically increase partner dependence, elevating reputation and IP risks.

questions.stem: Two candidate assembly countries have similar wages and infrastructure. What additional screen does the CAGE framework insist you apply?

options.A: Select purely by tariff rates, ignoring culture and geography completely too
options.B: Select purely by size of the host population and income levels
options.C: Compare cultural, administrative, geographic, and economic distance to target market directly
options.D: Select purely by absolute GDP growth rate of the host country

questions.explanation: CAGE emphasizes relative distance between home/target and candidate countries, not only absolute attractiveness metrics. Distance often explains the real cost and risk differences between seemingly similar options.

questions.stem: Under the chapter’s value-creation logic, when should Apple avoid a costly relocation of assembly?

options.A: Refrain when cultural distance is low and shipping times are short
options.B: Refrain when added costs exceed added willingness-to-pay benefits (C>V) over time
options.C: Refrain when benefits exceed costs and margins stay positive (V>C) always
options.D: Refrain when local responsiveness is high and cost pressure is low

questions.explanation: A global move is justified when it increases economic value creation. If added costs (including coordination and quality risks) exceed added value, the move destroys value and should be avoided.

questions.stem: Using CAGE logic, why might a U.S. firm prefer Ireland over Portugal as an EU base?

options.A: Lower cultural distance via shared language and diaspora, easing coordination with staff
options.B: Lower administrative distance because Portugal is not in the EU at all
options.C: Lower economic distance because Ireland uses the U.S. dollar legally for trade
options.D: Lower geographic distance because Ireland is closer to Brazil by sea routes

questions.explanation: A shared language can materially reduce cultural distance and coordination costs. Both Ireland and Portugal are EU members, so the key differentiator in the textbook example is cultural distance (language and ties).

questions.stem: When components remain China-centric while assembly moves to India, which hidden cost becomes more salient per the chapter’s definition?

options.A: Higher brand premiums because ‘Made in India’ signals luxury globally now
options.B: Higher coordination costs across dispersed plants, a liability of foreignness effect
options.C: Lower coordination costs due to vertical integration inside one country alone
options.D: Lower IP risk because suppliers can reverse-engineer less easily than before

questions.explanation: The liability of foreignness includes added coordination costs across geographic distance. A split supply chain often increases complexity in logistics, quality control, and cross-border coordination.

questions.stem: Which statement best matches the chapter’s emphasis that ‘distance’ is not just mileage?

options.A: Distance equals only miles travelled; culture never affects performance for firms
options.B: Distance includes culture, administration, and economics—not only miles between nations today
options.C: Distance equals only language; other factors do not matter at all
options.D: Distance equals only GDP gaps; geography never affects trade volumes much

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that distance includes cultural, administrative/political, geographic, and economic components. Each can affect costs and risks of international expansion.

questions.stem: Which statement best reconciles ‘many firms are >50% globalized’ with ‘the world is only semi-globalized’?

options.A: A firm’s foreign revenues imply that cross-border internet traffic must be high
options.B: A semi-globalized world means firms cannot gain advantage from global expansion ever
options.C: A semi-globalized world implies cultural distance no longer affects trade outcomes today
options.D: A firm can be highly international even when overall globalization remains limited

questions.explanation: Firm-level globalization (revenue mix) can be high even if many global flows are still mostly domestic. Semi-globalization means borders still matter on average; it does not prevent international success.

questions.stem: Why does the chapter say the ‘sequential commitment’ entry-mode model fits some firms but not others?

options.A: Stage model fits only internet firms; manufacturers must start with acquisitions abroad
options.B: Stage model fits manufacturing firms; born-global digital firms may skip stages entirely
options.C: Stage model fits only retailers; producers cannot use exporting to test markets
options.D: Stage model fits all firms; every company must export before investing abroad

questions.explanation: Internet and born-global firms can scale cross-border rapidly without moving through the classic export→alliance→subsidiary sequence. Traditional manufacturers often do follow a staged commitment path.

questions.stem: A firm that manufactures in one country and sells directly to another via cross-border shipments (with few foreign assets) is using:

options.A: Franchising: replicate service outlets through local entrepreneurs abroad widely
options.B: Joint venture: share ownership with host partner in-market equally
options.C: Acquisition: purchase foreign factories and brands for local presence
options.D: Exporting: produce in one country, sell in another directly

questions.explanation: Exporting is producing in one country and selling in another. The other options involve deeper local asset commitments and/or shared governance structures.

questions.stem: A market looks attractive by income, but CAGE indicates very high distance costs. What is the most defensible implication?

options.A: Prefer farthest markets to maximize learning even if costs spike in early entry
options.B: Prefer closer CAGE markets when distance costs overwhelm market-size attractiveness in early entry
options.C: Choose by GDP alone because cultural frictions can be standardized away quickly everywhere
options.D: Ignore CAGE because high-income markets always guarantee high sales in early entry stages

questions.explanation: CAGE highlights that distance creates costs/risks that can dominate otherwise attractive markets. A nearer market can yield better realized performance even if its absolute GDP is lower.

questions.stem: Adding a Europe-based design hub that feeds trend insights into a global platform is best described as:

options.A: Multidomestic strategy by letting each country develop separate brands alone
options.B: Global standardization by eliminating any local input into product design
options.C: Polycentric innovation by adding regional design hubs feeding global platform
options.D: One-way innovation shipping HQ designs abroad with no feedback loops

questions.explanation: Polycentric innovation draws from multiple hubs. The distinguishing feature is meaningful two-way or multi-way learning rather than HQ-only innovation flows.

questions.stem: Fast-fashion models often require both ultra-low cost and rapid adaptation to local demand signals. In the cost–responsiveness framework, this points most strongly to:

options.A: International strategy exporting unchanged products with minimal local tailoring globally
options.B: Transnational strategy combining scale efficiencies with rapid local adaptation globally
options.C: Multidomestic strategy duplicating full operations in each national market globally
options.D: Global standardization competing solely on lowest unit cost worldwide today

questions.explanation: High pressure for cost reductions plus high pressure for local responsiveness implies a transnational strategy—simultaneously seeking global scale efficiencies and local adaptation.

questions.stem: For a fast-fashion ecosystem, world-class logistics providers, textile clusters, and digital marketing complementors most directly map to which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Factor conditions: abundant oil reserves enabling cheaper clothes production locally
options.B: Demand conditions: sophisticated home buyers demanding avant‑garde couture locally today
options.C: Competitive intensity: one protected champion with no local rivalry pressure
options.D: Related industries: strong logistics, textiles, and digital marketing complementors locally

questions.explanation: Related and supporting industries (including complementors) strengthen national competitive advantage by providing inputs, know-how, and ecosystem capabilities that support the focal industry.

questions.stem: For cross-border platforms, EU data-privacy and consumer-protection enforcement differences most directly map to which CAGE dimension?

options.A: Economic distance from GDP gaps between rich and poor markets
options.B: Administrative distance from data-privacy rules and consumer-protection enforcement shifts quickly
options.C: Geographic distance from longer ocean routes between ports shifts quickly
options.D: Cultural distance from different fashion colours and seasonal rituals alone

questions.explanation: Regulatory requirements and enforcement institutions are administrative/political distance, and they can drive major compliance cost and risk differences across otherwise similar markets.

questions.stem: If Shein acquired a European retailer for quick legitimacy and distribution, which trade-off is most accurate per the entry-mode continuum?

options.A: Higher control and speed, but higher capital and integration risk for that deal
options.B: Higher control and speed, but lower capital and minimal integration risk for deal
options.C: Lower control and speed, but lower capital and minimal integration risk for deal
options.D: Lower control and speed, but higher capital and integration risk for that deal

questions.explanation: Acquisitions are high-control, high-investment moves that can provide speed (assets, channels) but create integration challenges and require substantial capital commitments.

questions.stem: If Shein builds and owns EU fulfillment centers to speed delivery and manage returns, that shift is best characterized as:

options.A: Licensing agreement granting brand rights to local platform sellers
options.B: Greenfield subsidiary building owned logistics and fulfillment assets there
options.C: Franchising model for apparel outlets run by independent operators
options.D: Pure exporting with no assets and no local employees

questions.explanation: Owned fulfillment centers are value-chain assets abroad, consistent with FDI through a subsidiary (often greenfield). Licensing/franchising rely more on partners; pure exporting avoids foreign assets.

questions.stem: If Shein buys a 20% stake in a European logistics start-up to secure capacity, what entry arrangement is most accurately described?

options.A: Equity alliance using minority ownership to secure strategic access
options.B: Licensing contract giving logistics partner rights to Shein brand
options.C: Joint venture using fifty-fifty ownership to create new company
options.D: Exporting arrangement shipping garments through independent carriers only there

questions.explanation: A minority equity stake to secure strategic access is an equity alliance. A joint venture implies shared control and often a new entity; licensing and exporting are non-equity arrangements.

questions.stem: If Shein licensed its designs and brand to local producers, which risk would typically rise most sharply?

options.A: IP protection improves because licensees have no access to design files
options.B: Tariff exposure disappears because licensing is always treated as domestic abroad
options.C: Coordination costs vanish because licensees report directly to headquarters abroad always
options.D: Brand reputation risk rises if licensees cut corners on quality abroad

questions.explanation: Licensing trades speed and low investment for reduced control. That often increases brand and quality variance, which heightens reputational risk—especially in consumer-facing categories.

questions.stem: If Shein shifts from pure cross-border shipping to owned EU warehouses, which change is most consistent with moving rightward on the investment/control continuum?

options.A: More control over delivery and returns, but less fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.B: Less control over delivery and returns, but less fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.C: More control over delivery and returns, but more fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.D: Less control over delivery and returns, but more fixed-cost commitment in each region

questions.explanation: Owned assets typically increase control over service quality and operational execution, but they also add fixed costs and capital commitment—making exit harder if the strategy fails.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization evidence, what share of voice-calling minutes are cross-border?

options.A: Only nine percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.B: Only eighteen percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.C: Only three percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.D: Only two percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today

questions.explanation: The chapter uses very low cross-border calling shares (about 2%) as one indicator that the world is not ‘fully flat’ but semi-globalized.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization indicators, what share of the world’s population are first-generation immigrants?

options.A: Twenty-five percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.B: Fifteen percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.C: Three percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.D: Nine percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide

questions.explanation: The chapter uses several low cross-border shares to argue the world is only semi-globalized; one of them is that only about 3% of the world’s population are first-generation immigrants.

questions.stem: Localizing size charts, payment methods, and return policies primarily addresses which pressure in the cost–responsiveness framework?

options.A: Cost-reduction pressure from duplicating warehouses and teams in every country abroad
options.B: Demand-conditions effect from sophisticated domestic customers in the home market alone
options.C: Local responsiveness pressure from different sizing norms and return expectations abroad
options.D: Factor-conditions effect from natural resources that support lower material cost abroad

questions.explanation: These actions tailor the offering and customer experience to local preferences and requirements, indicating pressure for local responsiveness (often supporting differentiation).

questions.stem: Policy changes that remove low-value shipping exemptions and tighten customs treatment primarily increase which kind of ‘distance’ in CAGE terms?

options.A: Cultural distance rises when parcel size preferences differ by region abruptly
options.B: Administrative distance rises when customs rules change for small parcels abruptly
options.C: Geographic distance rises when air freight becomes slower, not faster abruptly
options.D: Economic distance rises when incomes converge across consumer markets abruptly today

questions.explanation: Customs and tax treatments are political-institutional rules. Changing them raises administrative distance and can undermine the economics of cross-border direct-to-consumer fulfillment.

questions.stem: Public scrutiny of supply-chain practices that could reduce valuation and trigger consumer backlash is most closely linked to which downside of going global?

options.A: Loss of reputation if governance controversies spill into new markets
options.B: Liability of foreignness if tariff costs vanish and trust rises
options.C: Loss of IP if contract makers copy proprietary designs abroad
options.D: Location economies if overseas factories raise costs and reduce flexibility

questions.explanation: Reputational loss is a key disadvantage of global expansion, especially when supply chains cross jurisdictions with different labor, compliance, and transparency norms that attract public and regulatory attention.

questions.stem: Shein needing clearance from multiple regulators for a London IPO most directly illustrates which CAGE dimension?

options.A: Economic distance from income gaps between UK and China buyers listing
options.B: Administrative distance from cross-border securities rules and state approvals for listings
options.C: Cultural distance from fashion tastes between Asia and Europe for listings
options.D: Geographic distance from shipping routes between Guangzhou and London for listings

questions.explanation: Capital-market permissions, offshore listing rules, and state approvals are institutional and political barriers—administrative distance. They can shape feasibility even when customers, tastes, and physical shipping are unchanged.

questions.stem: Shein’s reported supplier diversification toward Brazil and Turkey most closely resembles which ‘why go global’ motive from the chapter?

options.A: Access larger consumer market by relocating suppliers, not sales today
options.B: Access low-cost inputs while reducing policy exposure in China today
options.C: Eliminate liability of foreignness by staying within one country today
options.D: Develop new competencies by entering biotech clusters for research today

questions.explanation: Shifting suppliers is primarily about input economics and risk-adjusted cost—access to cost-effective production capacity while hedging policy shocks tied to one geography.

questions.stem: Shipping delays and return frictions that materially affect economics most directly contradict which assumption discussed in the chapter?

options.A: Globalization hypothesis that tastes converge across countries much for firms today
options.B: Porter diamond where domestic rivalry raises firm competitiveness strongly over time
options.C: Liability of foreignness that entrants face extra coordination costs over distance
options.D: Death-of-distance hypothesis that geography no longer affects competitiveness much for firms

questions.explanation: The death-of-distance hypothesis suggests geography should not matter much for advantage. Persistent logistics frictions (time, cost, reliability) show geography remains consequential.

questions.stem: The additional compliance overhead and coordination costs Shein faces when operating under unfamiliar EU rules are best captured by:

options.A: Experience curve from output doubling to reduce unit costs
options.B: Location economies from locating activity in the best geography
options.C: Liability of foreignness from compliance and coordination in settings
options.D: Economies of scale from serving markets with same platform

questions.explanation: Liability of foreignness refers to extra costs of operating in unfamiliar environments and coordinating across distance. Compliance regimes and coordination complexity are classic sources of this liability.

questions.stem: When counterfeit versions of designs proliferate in a foreign market, which disadvantage of going global is most directly highlighted?

options.A: IP loss rises when designs get copied and scaled locally
options.B: Liability costs fall when firms enter culturally distant markets quickly
options.C: Location economies vanish when firms move production nearer to customers
options.D: Reputation risk rises when sales growth causes overcapacity in factories

questions.explanation: The chapter highlights loss of intellectual property as a downside of operating internationally, especially when local actors can copy, reverse-engineer, or counterfeit products and designs.

questions.stem: Which option best captures ‘globalization’ as defined in the chapter?

options.A: Purely cultural convergence where languages merge into one global dialect over time
options.B: Complete disappearance of borders making firms identical across all markets everywhere today
options.C: Closer cross-country integration enabled by lower barriers and cheaper coordination technology overall
options.D: Only rising tariffs and higher shipping costs reducing all trade volumes now

questions.explanation: Globalization is closer integration and exchange among countries, enabled by falling barriers and advances in telecommunications and transportation. It does not imply borders vanish entirely.

questions.stem: Which option best matches the chapter’s definition of a multinational enterprise (MNE)?

options.A: MNE: deploys resources to procure, produce, and distribute in ≥2 countries
options.B: MNE: sells only domestically but imports some inputs occasionally for production
options.C: MNE: earns revenue abroad but has no operations outside home base
options.D: MNE: holds foreign stocks but does not manage any subsidiaries abroad

questions.explanation: An MNE deploys resources/capabilities in procurement, production, and/or distribution in at least two countries. Mere foreign revenue or portfolio holdings are not sufficient by themselves.

questions.stem: Which option is the best definition of ‘global strategy’ as used in the chapter?

options.A: Corporate-level choices to compete and win against firms worldwide over time
options.B: Business-level choice to price below rivals in one local market only
options.C: Operational choice to schedule shifts on a single factory line only
options.D: Functional choice to design advertising slogans for one country audience only

questions.explanation: Global strategy is part of corporate strategy aimed at gaining and sustaining advantage while competing globally—across foreign and domestic rivals and multiple countries.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a joint venture from an equity alliance in the chapter’s entry-mode menu?

options.A: Equity alliance forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules
options.B: Licensing forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules today
options.C: Exporting forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules today
options.D: Joint venture forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules

questions.explanation: A joint venture typically creates a separate entity with shared ownership and governance. An equity alliance involves ownership stakes without necessarily forming a new jointly owned operating entity.

questions.stem: A dense cluster of specialized semiconductor suppliers, tooling, and advanced packaging expertise best maps to which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Factor conditions from large oil reserves financing chip fabrication plants there
options.B: Related industries with dense supplier clusters, tooling, and packaging expertise nearby
options.C: Demand conditions from domestic Taiwan consumers buying many high-end chips alone
options.D: Competitive intensity absent, with one protected firm and no rivals there

questions.explanation: Related and supporting industries (and complementors) strengthen national competitive advantage by providing ecosystem capabilities. Semiconductor competitiveness often depends on clusters of suppliers and specialized services.

questions.stem: Centralizing R&D and production for scale, while offering only compliance-driven variants by market, is closest to which global strategy?

options.A: Global standardization emphasizing scale, centralized R&D, and minimal localization overall today
options.B: Transnational strategy emphasizing deep localization plus global integration simultaneously overall today
options.C: Multidomestic strategy emphasizing independent country labs and production footprints overall today
options.D: International strategy emphasizing exports from home and low cost pressure only

questions.explanation: Global standardization focuses on scale and centralized activities to reduce cost. Small compliance variants do not necessarily imply a transnational approach unless local adaptation is deep and systematic.

questions.stem: Export controls and licensing constraints are a clear example of which CAGE distance being ‘weaponised’?

options.A: Geographic distance shaped by longer flights between chip fabs
options.B: Economic distance shaped by income gaps between data-center buyers
options.C: Administrative distance shaped by security-driven trade and export rules
options.D: Cultural distance shaped by language barriers between engineers alone

questions.explanation: Export rules are political-institutional barriers. They increase administrative distance by constraining what can be sold, to whom, and under what monitoring and enforcement regime.

questions.stem: For Nvidia, export controls most directly reduce which textbook advantage of competing internationally?

options.A: Developing new competencies becomes impossible because engineers cannot travel freely today
options.B: Access to low-cost inputs becomes impossible because chips are heavy today
options.C: Location economies vanish because every country has identical capabilities now already
options.D: Access to larger markets becomes constrained by export licensing caps today

questions.explanation: Export controls restrict market access regardless of customer demand, directly undermining the ‘larger market’ advantage. Input-factor access and competence building can still occur, though with added friction.

questions.stem: If hardware exports are constrained, a firm might consider technology licensing to local partners. Which trade-off is most accurate?

options.A: Higher capital, slower access, but lower IP risk and higher control overall risk
options.B: Lower capital, faster access, but higher IP leakage and control loss overall risk
options.C: Lower capital, faster access, but lower IP risk and higher control overall risk
options.D: Higher capital, slower access, but higher IP leakage and control loss overall risk

questions.explanation: Licensing is low-investment and can speed presence, but it reduces control and can increase IP leakage risk. Higher-control modes protect IP better but require more capital and may be blocked by policy.

questions.stem: If the world bifurcates into rival technology blocs, what global-strategy implication is most defensible for MNEs?

options.A: Prepare only marketing adaptation because hardware trade barriers will disappear over time
options.B: Prepare single global supply chain because blocs always reconverge quickly over time
options.C: Prepare to exit all foreign markets because semi-globalization forbids trade over time
options.D: Prepare dual supply chains and standards for separate geopolitical blocs over time

questions.explanation: Strategic bifurcation can force firms to operate parallel supply chains, standards, and compliance regimes. Single-stack assumptions become fragile when policy and standards diverge by bloc.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s CAGE discussion, how does geographic distance affect trade volume in the cited comparison?

options.A: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade only with identical languages and cultures today always
options.B: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade about one‑fifth as much as 1,000 mile pairs
options.C: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade about twice as much as nearby pairs today
options.D: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade the same as any distance at all today

questions.explanation: The chapter uses distance elasticities to show that geography still matters: longer distances sharply reduce trade volumes, even before adding cultural and administrative distances.

questions.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization indicators, what share of internet traffic crosses national borders?

options.A: Eighteen percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.B: Seventy percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.C: Thirty percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.D: Fifty percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today

questions.explanation: The chapter cites that only about 18% of internet traffic is cross-border, reinforcing the argument that the world remains semi-globalized rather than fully ‘flat.’

questions.stem: Locating an AI research lab in a top talent cluster to learn faster is best explained by which concept?

options.A: Globalization hypothesis from converging tastes for AI chips globally
options.B: Liability of foreignness from operating only in domestic markets
options.C: Location economies from placing R&D where talent clusters concentrate
options.D: Economies of scale from serving markets with same platform

questions.explanation: Location economies refer to benefits from locating a specific value-chain activity in the geography that offers the best conditions for that activity—here, talent and knowledge spillovers.

questions.stem: Monitoring and inspection requirements attached to exports primarily add what, according to the chapter’s concept set?

options.A: Reduced compliance costs, weakening liability of foreignness abroad for exporters over time
options.B: Lower factor conditions, reducing infrastructure and human capital in host for chips
options.C: Higher demand conditions in home market, improving national competitive advantage for chips
options.D: Added compliance and coordination costs, strengthening liability of foreignness abroad for exporters

questions.explanation: Compliance-heavy exporting and cross-border coordination increase the costs of operating across jurisdictions, consistent with liability of foreignness (unfamiliar institutions and coordination across distance).

questions.stem: Pursuing country-specific chip variants to satisfy local rules can undermine which benefit associated with cost reductions?

options.A: It can eliminate regulatory risk, making tariffs irrelevant to strategy overall
options.B: It can create location economies by centralizing everything in one country
options.C: It can erode scale economies, raising unit costs of production overall
options.D: It can remove cultural distance, aligning buyer preferences across markets overall

questions.explanation: High local responsiveness often increases costs by fragmenting volumes and duplicating efforts, which can erode scale economies. This is one reason balancing both pressures is difficult.

questions.stem: Rising wages in an offshoring destination can have what effect on the original ‘low-cost input factor’ advantage?

options.A: Rising wages remove cultural distance, aligning preferences across all nations today fully
options.B: Rising wages make administrative distance disappear, removing tariffs worldwide at once today
options.C: Rising wages can expand low-cost advantages, making offshoring more attractive to China
options.D: Rising wages can erode low-cost advantages that first motivated offshoring to China

questions.explanation: As wages rise, the cost advantage that motivated offshoring can shrink or disappear, prompting firms to re-optimise location choices or invest in automation and productivity.

questions.stem: The chapter highlights U.S.–China ‘codependence’ in trade and technology. Which pairing best matches that claim?

options.A: U.S. depends on China for oil exports; China depends on U.S. for rice imports
options.B: U.S. depends on China for language services; China depends on West for tourism only
options.C: U.S. depends on China for manufactured goods; China depends on West for chips designs
options.D: U.S. depends on China for aircraft engines; China depends on West for snow sports

questions.explanation: The chapter’s argument is that interdependence remains deep: the U.S. relies on Chinese manufacturing, while China still depends on advanced Western technologies such as cutting-edge chip design and equipment.

questions.stem: The chapter notes that only a small share of an iPhone’s value is added in final assembly. What is that approximate share?

options.A: About fifty percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.B: About five percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.C: About fifteen percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.D: About thirty percent of iPhone value is added in assembly

questions.explanation: The chapter uses the iPhone example to show how little value can be captured by low-margin assembly relative to upstream design and key components, reinforcing the ‘Designed vs Made’ distinction.

questions.stem: The chapter’s note that cutting-edge chip supply is concentrated in one geography implies what strategic risk for MNEs?

options.A: Supply concentration eliminates risk because one supplier guarantees uniform standards always everywhere
options.B: Supply concentration mainly increases cultural distance between buyers and engineers in chips
options.C: Supply concentration lowers costs but also removes any need for inventory buffers
options.D: Supply concentration raises geopolitical risk; disruption can halt global electronics quickly today

questions.explanation: When critical supply is geographically concentrated, firms face geopolitical and operational disruption risk (e.g., conflict, sanctions, logistics shocks). This is a global-strategy vulnerability beyond simple cost calculus.

questions.stem: U.S. export controls that force Nvidia to redesign China-facing chips primarily increase which pressure in the cost–responsiveness framework?

options.A: Pressure for local responsiveness due to converging global consumer tastes alone
options.B: Pressure for cost reductions due to scale economies in one design
options.C: Pressure for cost reductions due to higher wages in home country
options.D: Pressure for local responsiveness due to host-country requirements and constraints rising

questions.explanation: In the chapter, local responsiveness includes tailoring to host-country requirements—not only consumer tastes. Export controls are regulatory requirements that force product tailoring by market, raising local-responsiveness pressure.

questions.stem: Under techno cold war conditions, what new screening factor becomes central in ‘where to compete’ decisions?

options.A: Country choice should be random because distance never influences global outcomes today
options.B: Country choice should focus solely on geographic proximity to headquarters today only
options.C: Country choice must include political alignment, not only market potential anymore today
options.D: Country choice can ignore politics because trade rules are stable worldwide today

questions.explanation: When export controls and security logics spread across blocs, political alignment and policy predictability become decisive constraints alongside economic attractiveness and CAGE distances.

questions.stem: When an international partner uses transferred know-how to create competing products and undercut the original firm, which downside of going global is most directly illustrated?

options.A: Loss of intellectual property when partners learn and compete globally after transfer
options.B: Liability of foreignness when firms avoid foreign markets and stay home always
options.C: Location economies when firms relocate activity to optimal geographies worldwide for savings
options.D: Loss of reputation when partners mistreat workers and damage brand after transfer

questions.explanation: The chapter’s IP-loss examples show how partners can ‘learn’ and then compete. This is distinct from reputational loss and from the generic foreignness costs of operating abroad.

questions.stem: When export controls make one market risky, the most defensible reallocation principle is to:

options.A: Reallocate scarce output to markets with lowest geographic distance only always
options.B: Reallocate scarce output to markets with lower administrative distance and certainty
options.C: Reallocate output to markets with equal distance, since distance never matters
options.D: Reallocate scarce output to markets with higher administrative distance and uncertainty

questions.explanation: Administrative distance and policy predictability can dominate other attractiveness metrics under export controls. Firms tend to prioritize markets where rules are clearer and enforcement risk lower.

questions.stem: Which condition most strongly supports a global-standardization approach for a technology product?

options.A: When customer needs differ strongly and governments mandate local adaptation globally today
options.B: When costs are irrelevant because buyers pay any price for chips globally
options.C: When suppliers are local monopolies and firms can ignore rivals easily globally
options.D: When customer needs are similar and scale economies are large globally today

questions.explanation: Global standardization fits when customer needs are relatively homogeneous and scale economies are large, making centralized, standardized offerings cost-effective.

questions.stem: Which difference from the earlier Cold War is emphasized in the chapter’s ‘techno cold war’ framing?

options.A: Unlike USSR, China relies only on oil exports and not technology imports today
options.B: Unlike USSR, China depends on U.S. protection alliances to sustain growth today overall
options.C: Unlike USSR, China is isolated economically and trades little with U.S today overall
options.D: Unlike USSR, China rivals U.S. GDP and is trade‑interdependent in critical goods today

questions.explanation: The chapter highlights both China’s near-peer economic scale and deep U.S.–China codependence in trade and technology, distinguishing the techno cold war from the USSR-era Cold War.

questions.stem: Which entry mode gives the highest design/control over facilities and culture, but often the slowest ramp-up?

options.A: Greenfield subsidiary: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice
options.B: Franchising: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today
options.C: Exporting: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today
options.D: Licensing: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today

questions.explanation: Greenfield subsidiaries require building from scratch, which is slower but allows the firm to design operations and culture. Exporting/licensing/franchising are lower-investment and do not provide the same facility control.

questions.stem: Which motive for going global is most directly served when an MNE relocates R&D to join a learning cluster?

options.A: Access low-cost inputs by relocating production to higher-wage areas for advantage
options.B: Develop new competencies by embedding in global learning communities for advantage
options.C: Avoid all foreign risks by keeping operations strictly domestic for advantage
options.D: Access larger markets by reducing administrative distance via tariffs for advantage

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that firms often expand internationally to develop new competencies by joining communities of learning in specific regions (clusters), especially for differentiation-driven advantages.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the chapter’s claim about national competitive advantage?

options.A: World-leading home industries guarantee firms face no liability of foreignness abroad ever
options.B: World-leading home industries imply geography never matters for competitive advantage again today
options.C: World-leading home industries prevent firms from expanding because markets saturate quickly abroad
options.D: World-leading home industries produce firms that compete strongest internationally over many years

questions.explanation: National competitive advantage—world leadership in specific industries—tends to produce globally strong competitors. It does not eliminate foreignness liabilities, nor does it make geography irrelevant.

questions.stem: Within Porter’s diamond, what is the most direct mechanism by which intense domestic rivalry helps global competitiveness?

options.A: Domestic rivalry reduces innovation because firms collude and avoid competition there
options.B: Domestic rivalry matters only when customers abroad are sophisticated buyers there
options.C: Domestic rivalry pushes rapid innovation, strengthening global competitiveness of firms there
options.D: Domestic rivalry matters only when natural resources are abundant there always

questions.explanation: Competitive intensity at home pressures firms to improve, innovate, and contain costs—capabilities that can translate into stronger performance in global markets.
